paragraphs.heading: Forecasting with equations
paragraphs.text: Numerical weather prediction, or NWP, forecasts the weather by feeding current conditions into mathematical models of the atmosphere and oceans. The idea is to take a snapshot of the air at one moment, then apply the laws of fluid dynamics and thermodynamics, written as equations, to work out how it will look later. Loading observations into the model to set its starting state is called initialization.

paragraphs.heading: Where the data comes from
paragraphs.text: Models run in many countries take in observations from radiosondes, weather satellites and other systems. Radiosondes are devices carried by weather balloons that climb through the troposphere well into the stratosphere, measuring the air and sending the results to a fixed receiver. The World Meteorological Organization standardizes instruments, methods and timing worldwide. Because the observations are unevenly spaced, data assimilation checks their quality and turns them into values at points the model can use, and these become the forecast's starting point.

paragraphs.heading: Limits on accuracy
paragraphs.text: NWP needs some of the most powerful supercomputers in the world, yet its forecast skill reaches only about six days. Accuracy depends on how dense and good the observations are, and on flaws in the models themselves. A deeper problem is that the equations describing the atmosphere are chaotic. They cannot be solved exactly, and small errors grow, doubling roughly every five days. Even with perfect data and a flawless model, this limits accurate forecasts to about 14 days.

paragraphs.heading: Coping with uncertainty
paragraphs.text: The equations must be supplemented with parameterizations for things like solar radiation, clouds and rain, soil, vegetation and terrain. Model output also misses some details near the ground, so in the 1970s and 1980s a statistical link between model output and the conditions that follow at the surface was built, called model output statistics (MOS). Since the 1990s, ensemble forecasts, which analyze many forecasts from one model or several, have helped gauge confidence and stretch useful forecasts further ahead.

paragraphs.heading: From hand sums to ENIAC
paragraphs.text: In the 1920s Lewis Fry Richardson, using methods developed by Vilhelm Bjerknes, worked out by hand a six-hour forecast for two points in central Europe, which took him at least six weeks. In 1950 the ENIAC produced the first forecasts made by computer, using a much simplified version of the equations. In 1954 Carl-Gustav Rossby's group in Sweden used the same model for the first operational forecast, meaning a routine one for practical use. The United States followed in 1955 with a joint unit of its Air Force, Navy and Weather Bureau.

paragraphs.heading: Climate models
paragraphs.text: Models built on the same physics can produce either short-term forecasts or long-term climate predictions, and the latter are widely used to understand and project climate change. In 1956 Norman Phillips built a model that realistically showed monthly and seasonal patterns in the troposphere, the first successful climate model. In the late 1960s, NOAA's Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory built the first general circulation climate model to combine ocean and atmosphere.
